newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Boy Wonder of Russia politics weathers first storm.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Boy Wonder of Russia politics weathers first storm.

text.p: The urgently awaited phone call from Moscow came while Boris Nemtsov was in full flow, denouncing the evils of the old command economy and proudly enumerating the new Russian government's achievements.

Calmly, Nemtsov finished his remarks and, after taking the call, emerged into bright summer sunshine to shake hands with the people of this depressed northern town and parry their complaints about life in Russia's brave capitalist new world.
The golden boy of Russian politics was in his element, moving among the common people trying to win them to his cause with a blend of straight-talking, quick humour and boyish charm.

Only on the plane back to Moscow afterwards did it become clear that Nemtsov, seen by many as a future president, had just weathered his biggest test since being drafted into the cabinet last March to help revive Russia's stalled reform programme.
"The president is satisfied with the sale of the stake in Svyazinvest and with the large sum of money it has raised...Things will settle down now," said Nemtsov, grinning broadly.
NEMTSOV STANDS GROUND IN SVYAZINVEST ROW

His relief was understandable. Boris Yeltsin's endorsement of the sale of a quarter of Russia's state telecommunications giant followed a series of unprecedented attacks on the young liberal by newspapers and television channels belonging to media magnates reportedly backing a rival bid for the stake.

Prominent ORT television presenter Sergei Dorenko said he believed Nemtsov had acted incorrectly over Svyazinvest and said he was "twitching" like a "cockroach". The empire of one of the magnates, Boris Berezovsky, has a major stake in ORT.
As the recriminations over Svyazinvest mounted, Nemtsov, on a hectic three-day swing through the provinces, stuck to his guns and blasted the losers of the auction as "bandit capitalists".

"There will be no more sales of state property on the cheap, no more privileged conditions for certain companies," he said, referring to previous shady deals cut with powerful financial groupings during Russia's controversial privatisation process.

"The winner (of future sell-offs) will be the one who pays the most," Nemtsov said. The money would go into the state's depleted coffers to help pay Russia's impoverished doctors, teachers, soldiers and pensioners, he said.

Debates about company shares and the astronomical sums paid for them can sound very abstract to ordinary Russians struggling to feed themselves and their families but Nemtsov, an astute politician, showed he had the popular touch.
"I don't want to live in a country of bandits and neither, I am sure, do you," he told a gathering in the Siberian city of Novosibirsk on another stopover in his provinicial tour.

Many Russians have seen their living standards plunge since the fall of communism and believe the only beneficiaries of reform have been criminal gangs snatching up the country's most lucrative assets with the connivance of the authorities.
Nemtsov's energy, good looks and refreshing lack of pomposity impressed many of his listeners, especially the women.
"He's a good lad, he could do a lot of good but he is only one against many," said factory worker Galina Vladimirovna.
Another supporter, Galina Papsheva, said: "I think he has all the makings of a president."
AMBITIOUS NEMTSOV KEEPS FOCUS ON IMMEDIATE ISSUES

Voted Russia's most trusted politician in a survey conducted when he joined the government, Nemtsov has played down talk of his running for president in the next election, due in 2000. Yeltsin himself cannot stand for a third term.
But there can be no mistaking the ambition and drive of the First Deputy Prime Minister, who is still only 37.
"We have paid off our arrears to the pensioners, we will pay our debts to the military by September and to the doctors and teachers by January," he said in Novosibirsk.

The government had cut railway tariffs to help revive the economy of remote regions like Siberia and the Russian Far East. It would also bring in a fairer taxation system and hack away at the red tape that has long hampered Russian business, he said.

Clearly much impressed by his recent trip to nominally communist China, Nemtsov said the Chinese had understood what Russia's still powerful Communist Party had failed to grasp. "There is no alternative to the market economy."

Nemtsov, whose wide range of responsibilites include energy, housing reform and shaking up the huge Soviet-era utility companies, also pledged to bring more youthful and talented people into government.
"As Stalin said, personnel decide everything," he said, mischievously quoting the Soviet dictator for the benefit of his mostly elderly audience.
NEEDS YELTSIN'S GOODWILL, CHUBAIS' BACKING

Nemtsov has brought some young liberal allies with him from Nizhny Novgorod -- where he was governor before joining the cabinet -- but he still lacks a solid power base in Moscow and so remains vulnerable when rows like Svyazinvest flare up.

Yeltsin, who tipped Nemtsov as possible presidential material as long as three years ago, is personally fond of his protege -- they are both engineers by profession -- but wants him to prove his mettle, well-informed sources said.
Perhaps equally crucial to Nemtsov's fortunes is Anatoly Chubais, another First Deputy Prime Minister who also runs the finance ministry in Yeltsin's reshuffled team.

Chubais, a brilliant administrator who spearheaded Russia's privatisation programme and ran Yeltsin's re-election campaign last year, is not expected to seek the presidency himself because of his unpopularity but is seen as a kingmaker.
The sources said the Svyazinvest scandal had driven the two reformers into a closer alliance and both Chubais and Nemtsov understood their survival rested on the other.
Laughing off the recent tensions, Nemtsov told Reuters that the most important thing was getting the government's message across to the ordinary people.
Asked whether he worried about making powerful enemies so early on in his Moscow career, he replied with a philosophical shrug: "That is what politics is all about. It can't be helped."
